forces: Two violins, two violas and two cellos
performers: Hollywood String Quartet (Felix Slatkin and Paul Shure, violins; Paul Robyn, viola; Eleanor Aller, cello); Alvin Dinkin, viola; Kurt Reher, cello
question: What changes when an earlier phrase returns with a different harmony and a lighter accompaniment?
intro: The man’s answer begins in D major: he accepts the child, and earlier musical ideas acquire a different setting. This is the continuation of one sextet, not its second movement. The LP break falls between bars 228 and 229; this side begins at bar 229 and carries the work through its quiet conclusion at bar 418.

cues.title: An answer in D major
cues.text: The side opens with a broad D-major sonority in violas and cellos. It answers the suspended B♭ at the end of side 1: the tonal change belongs to the man’s acceptance in Dehmel’s poem, not to a new movement.
cues.evidence: Original sextet score, bars 228–234, ASC E1 pp. 25–26, inspected; Schoenberg’s analysis identifies the D-major answer. The analysed side starts in the corresponding D-major region, after the first side’s B♭ tail.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A line inside the chord
cues.text: Follow the cello’s moving phrase as the broad opening sonority loosens into separate voices. The answer is not one static major chord: the same six players continue to exchange and transform melodic material.
cues.evidence: Original score p. 26, bars 229–240, gives the first cello an expressive line as the violins enter. The report changes at 0:36 and becomes less forceful after the first half-minute; placement is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Emotion rather than stage directions
cues.text: In his notes, Schoenberg said the work was not trying to illustrate an action or a drama, but nature and human feeling. That distinction matters here: the poem gives a framework without assigning every instrumental gesture a literal event.
cues.evidence: Schoenberg’s 1950 programme note is reproduced on the original Capitol sleeve and at the Arnold Schönberg Center: https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Muted strings and harmonics
cues.text: The quieter moonlit passage changes the strings’ colour. Mutes soften the sound; harmonics and light running figures create a different surface from the broad lower-string statement that opened the side.
cues.evidence: Original sextet score p. 27, bars 249–250, explicitly marks mutes and harmonics; Schoenberg’s analysis connects this texture with moonlight. The report’s quieter 1:35–2:10 region supports approximate placement, not the exact moment a mute is fitted.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Lightness is still activity
cues.text: Do not equate this lighter colour with an absence of movement. Listen beneath the longer phrase for small, quickly moving figures, then notice how their presence changes the way a sustained note is heard.
cues.evidence: The original score and composer’s analysis distinguish light runs from sustained and harmonic tones. This cue offers a listening strategy without claiming a particular run at 2:32.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The quiet texture expands
cues.text: The lighter passage grows into another stronger wave. The change comes from the six strings themselves, not from added wind or brass colour; compare the phrase’s weight with its earlier, muted setting.
cues.evidence: The report has strong changes at 2:36, 2:42 and 3:04, with a level rise around 2:50–2:55. The cue describes the surrounding expansion, not an exact thematic transformation.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Earlier ideas find new company
cues.text: The later half brings earlier themes into new combinations. Instead of hearing the music as a sequence of unrelated tunes, compare the shape of a phrase with the harmony and counterline now surrounding it.
cues.evidence: Schoenberg’s analysis explains transformed earlier themes and a violin–cello duet in the latter half. Report boundaries at 3:32 and 3:48 locate this broader active paragraph; no exact theme entry is assigned to the cue.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The poet heard independent music
cues.text: After hearing the work, Dehmel wrote to Schoenberg in December 1912 that he had forgotten to follow his poem because the music held him. The response supports hearing an instrumental argument as well as a literary programme.
cues.evidence: Dehmel’s letter of 12 December 1912 is quoted in the Arnold Schönberg Center essay: https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4. This is a paraphrase, not a fabricated direct quotation.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A renewed broad crest
cues.text: The recombined material rises to another substantial crest and then recedes. Listen for continuity across the decrease: an expressive phrase can remain in progress after its loudest point has passed.
cues.evidence: The report has a strong window around 5:00, with structural-change peaks at 4:52 and 5:12. The surrounding decrease supports the broad contour only.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A melody can change its role
cues.text: A figure first heard as a prominent melody may later sit inside the texture. Try listening for a familiar contour in the middle voices rather than expecting every return at the top of the ensemble.
cues.evidence: The original six-part score and composer’s analysis establish recombination and thematic transformation. No particular inner-voice return is asserted at 5:42.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The paragraph changes colour
cues.text: A new turn in the passage changes the balance of the sound without stopping the continuous movement. Listen for a softer arrival as carefully as for an emphatic one.
cues.evidence: The report identifies a structural-change peak at 6:20, with changing spectral and tonal estimates in the surrounding windows. Those estimates are not promoted into a specific chord claim.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: The line broadens again
cues.text: The later phrase expands into a stronger D-major-coloured span. That return of tonal warmth is not yet the final ending: the music will still withdraw and recombine its earlier material.
cues.evidence: The report rises around 7:10–7:20 and places D-major pitch classes prominently there. Schoenberg’s analysis establishes D major as the latter half’s tonal destination; this is not a bar-aligned tonic cadence.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Before the orchestral versions
cues.text: The six-player score was published in 1905. Schoenberg later arranged it for string orchestra in 1917 and revised that arrangement in 1943. This recording keeps the original chamber forces, so individual lines are carried by individuals rather than whole sections.
cues.evidence: Arnold Schönberg Center work catalogue lists the 1905 Dreililien first edition; the work essay distinguishes the 1917 and 1943 orchestral texts: https://archive2.schoenberg.at/compositions/werke_einzelansicht.php?werke_id=420&herkunft=allewerke; https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Listen across the retreat
cues.text: When the sound diminishes, keep following the shape of the phrase. A quiet continuation can preserve the earlier tension even while its surface becomes less insistent.
cues.evidence: The report is markedly quieter around 7:30–7:55 before renewed activity around 8:00. The cue concerns that passage-level contour, not a precise bow release.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Two low voices, different jobs
cues.text: The two cellos need not move together. One can support the harmony while the other participates in the melodic exchange; hearing both roles helps keep the sextet from becoming a melody with an anonymous bass.
cues.evidence: The original sextet score writes separate first and second cello lines throughout. This is a general ensemble-listening point, not a claim of a solo at 8:52.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Warmth before the coda
cues.text: The later part continues to gather and relax before the quiet coda. Keep the opening walking figure in memory: the ending will transform earlier ideas rather than discard them for an unrelated closing tune.
cues.evidence: The report changes at 9:34 and 10:06. Schoenberg’s analysis describes the final recombination of the opening and later themes; the cue anticipates it without locating a thematic entrance at 9:30.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The coda remembers differently
cues.text: In the coda, earlier material appears in a changed setting. The opening’s dark walk and the later answer are brought into relation; “transfiguration” means altered context as well as a change from minor to major.
cues.evidence: Schoenberg’s analysis describes the final coda’s transformed themes; original score pp. 44–45 gives the Sehr ruhig passage and interwoven lines. The strong 10:06 report change is the approximate coda marker, not an aligned bar number.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hollywood, August nineteen fifty
cues.text: The Arnold Schönberg Center dates these sessions to 21–22 August 1950 in Hollywood. Felix Slatkin, Paul Shure, Paul Robyn and Eleanor Aller were joined by Alvin Dinkin and Kurt Reher to make the six-player ensemble.
cues.evidence: Arnold Schönberg Audio Archive, recording 47, gives dates, Hollywood location and all six players: https://archive.schoenberg.at/av/aufnahme.php?id_aufnahme=47&action=view
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The last expansion subsides
cues.text: A final substantial wave has begun to fall away. Listen for how the line continues after the larger sound disappears, making the approach to the ending longer than a single closing chord.
cues.evidence: The report reaches a high level around 10:55, remains strong through 11:10, and drops sharply at 11:15; its strongest structural-change peak is 11:18. The cue sits in the following withdrawal.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: The quiet conclusion
cues.text: The closing passage sustains a low level while small figures continue beneath longer notes. The music does not become motionless as it becomes quiet; the final D-major settling is prepared by that continuing activity.
cues.evidence: The report changes at 11:58 and stays quiet through most of the remaining minute and a half. Original score pp. 50–51 shows moving inner figures beneath held upper notes and the D-major close.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Separate motion from volume
cues.text: At this reduced level, follow the quick inner motion rather than only the high sustained line. A soft texture can contain many notes without recovering the earlier agitation.
cues.evidence: Original score’s final pages keep arpeggiated inner figures under long upper notes. The report’s quiet late windows support the broad placement; scratch-sensitive onset counts are not treated as the number of musical attacks.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Let the last chord arrive
cues.text: The flowing inner figures eventually yield to the held closing sonority. Allow the final chord and its release to complete the work; the surface noise that remains belongs to the old disc, not to a seventh player.
cues.evidence: Original score p. 51 ends with a held D-major sonority after quiet running figures. The report registers a late change at 13:32 and a low tail near 13:45, within the 13:48.7 file. No exact final attack is asserted.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: D major gives way to muted light
transitions.how: After the broad D-major answer, the phrase slows and pauses before a quieter F♯-major passage. Schoenberg changes the colour from sustained lower-string weight to muted running figures and harmonics. The same six instruments now provide the moonlit surface described in his programme note; the contrast is both harmonic and instrumental.
transitions.evidence: Original score p. 27, bars 248–250: ritardando, fermata, mutes, harmonics and six-sharp key signature. The report’s quiet 1:35–2:10 region supports approximate placement; no precise first muted note is claimed.

transitions.title: The light texture opens into dialogue
transitions.how: The light, muted texture gives way to more sustained melodic exchanges and renewed expansion. Earlier ideas are brought into a new relation, including the violin–cello dialogue described by Schoenberg. Rather than introduce a new instrumental family, he redistributes melody and accompaniment among the existing six voices.
transitions.evidence: Schoenberg’s analysis, examples 12–14, describes the later duet and new warmth. The report changes at 3:32 and 3:48 with stronger windows around 3:50. The heading is a broad listening span, not the exact first duet bar.

transitions.title: Earlier themes enter a quieter setting
transitions.how: The later thematic span relaxes into the Sehr ruhig coda. A longer upper phrase, moving inner figures and a quieter bass can coexist without the earlier massed weight. The ending combines and changes the significance of familiar material: its continuity comes from thematic memory, not from an unrelated closing melody.
transitions.evidence: Original score pp. 44–45 and the composer’s account of the coda. The report has a strong change at 10:06 and further changes at 10:22; the marker is approximate and does not identify a particular cadence.

transitions.title: The final wave leaves moving inner voices
transitions.how: After the last expansion, the sextet reduces its weight while preserving motion in the inner parts. Long upper notes stretch over soft running figures before the final D-major sonority. Harmonic settling and the disappearance of sound are separate events: the quiet conclusion gives the listener time to hear both.
transitions.evidence: Original score pp. 50–51 supplies the closing texture and D-major endpoint. The report drops strongly after 11:10, changes at 11:58 and stays low through the ending; no exact final cadence time is claimed.

source.locator: pp. 26–27, 44–45, 50–51; bars 229–418. Each violin identifier is one player; “violas” and “cellos” each group two independent players. Approximate passage states.

timeline.note: The D-major answer opens in violas and cellos; the first cello develops the broad expressive line.
Violins join the lower strings as the opening answer unfolds into separate melodic strands.
Muted running violin figures pass against harmonics and light responses in the lower strings.
The complete sextet carries the later thematic exchanges; no single voice is asserted as continuously leading this long span.
The coda combines a long upper line and expressive cello motion with more active inner figures.
The quiet close retains a high sustained line over flowing inner strings before the final held chord.

composer.epithet: A Viennese teacher who took motivic development beyond the key signature, then made twelve notes carry the work of a tonal system.
facts: Largely self-taught; counterpoint lessons with Alexander Zemlinsky; close study of Bach, Beethoven, Brahms and Wagner
Berg and Webern from 1904 · Prussian Academy of Arts, Berlin, 1926–33 · University of California, Los Angeles, 1936–44
Developing variation · free atonality · twelve-tone composition · Sprechstimme
Painter; author of Harmonielehre (1911); founder of the Society for Private Musical Performances
composer.background:
Arnold Schoenberg was born in Vienna’s Leopoldstadt, the son of a Jewish shopkeeper, and learned the violin as a child. When his father died in 1889, the family’s finances made extended formal study impossible. He worked in a bank from 1891 to 1895, played chamber music with friends and learned composition by examining scores. Alexander Zemlinsky, whom he met through the amateur orchestra Polyhymnia, gave him counterpoint lessons. Schoenberg’s later teaching grew from this close reading: he explained, with unusual insistence, what each note in Bach, Mozart, Beethoven and Brahms was doing.

In the 1890s the apparent opposition between Brahms and Wagner organised Viennese musical argument. Schoenberg took techniques from both. From Brahms came the continuous alteration of a small motif, later described as developing variation; from Wagner came chromatic harmony whose resolution could be postponed across an entire scene. Verklärte Nacht, written in 1899 for string sextet, applies these procedures to Richard Dehmel’s poem about a woman confessing to her lover that she carries another man’s child. The opening D minor eventually transforms into D major, supplying the work’s large-scale harmonic argument.
